sketches.title: The Legend Gets Worse
sketches.premise: A family story is being told at dinner. Take turns adding the next true-sounding detail, making the legend grow without changing what has already been said. The host will notice if your brave little fact cannot stand on the shoulders of the last one.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it adds exactly one believable link to the same chain and fits the whole story; a skipped link jumps past what the last detail makes necessary, an ending declares the tale finished, and an undo cancels or rewrites an earlier fact.
sketches.move_shape: Add one next link, not a side story: “After Uncle Ray slipped, the birthday cake slid into the dog’s bowl.”
sketches.first_card: Grandma once won a prize at the county fair, but nobody remembers what it was.

sketches.title: And That Is How We Know
sketches.premise: The family is retelling one famous dinner disaster. Each turn adds one piece of proof for the claim already on the table, while leaving room for the next piece. Make your proof awkward, costly, or suspicious; merely saying “everyone agreed” earns the warm glow of nothing.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it adds one checkable piece that supports the same claim and fits every earlier piece; a skipped link offers proof with no needed bridge, an ending says the claim is settled, and an undo removes or denies a fact already used.
sketches.move_shape: Add one piece of proof: “The missing pie tin was found behind Dad’s chair, still warm.”
sketches.first_card: Everyone says the family’s quietest dinner was not quiet by choice.

sketches.title: The Recipe Nobody Wrote Down
sketches.premise: At dinner, the family rebuilds a legendary dish from memory, one step at a time. Add the next cooking step so the dish can still exist, then make your relative’s part harder, stranger, or mildly shameful. Do not suddenly serve the finished meal; even soup deserves a middle.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it adds exactly the next workable step to the same recipe and fits all stated ingredients, tools, and results; a skipped link jumps over a needed preparation, an ending serves or eats the dish, and an undo removes or changes an earlier step.
sketches.move_shape: Add one next cooking step: “While Aunt Jo stirred the sauce, she used the birthday candle as a spoon.”
sketches.first_card: The family’s famous picnic cake began with one egg, a dented bowl, and too much confidence.

sketches.title: The Caption Is the Family Story
sketches.premise: A strange family photo is passed around after dinner. Take turns adding the next fact that explains what is happening, keeping one shared story alive. Your best move makes somebody look foolish without putting the photo somewhere it plainly cannot be.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it adds one plausible moment or cause that fits the whole visible scene and earlier captions; a skipped link leaps over the action it claims to explain, an ending gives the final caption, and an undo says a shown detail was not there or happened differently.
sketches.move_shape: Add one scene-fitting moment: “Just before the flash, Dad hid the second shoe under the table.”
sketches.first_card: In the photo, Grandpa is wearing a crown, holding a broom, and looking offended.

sketches.title: The Toast That Went Sideways
sketches.premise: One family member gives a dinner toast, and the table remembers it one sentence at a time. Add the next sentence so it follows the last one, then slip in a detail that makes the speaker, listener, or occasion squirm. A new toast is not a next sentence, however tempting the escape.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it adds exactly one connected sentence to the same toast and fits its speaker, mood, occasion, and all prior sentences; a skipped link changes the subject without a bridge, an ending gives the toast’s sign-off, and an undo retracts an earlier sentence.
sketches.move_shape: Add the next sentence: “That was when I learned Uncle Ben had brought the wrong family a gift.”
sketches.first_card: At Grandma’s anniversary dinner, Dad raised his glass and said, “We should probably explain the smoke.”

sketches.title: Where That Thing Came From
sketches.premise: A family heirloom sits on the dinner table, and everyone tells its history backward, one owner at a time. Each move names the next believable hand it passed through and adds a small cost, secret, or insult for that owner. Do not skip to the famous first owner; the object has a history, even if it is mostly poor choices.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it names exactly the next connected owner or transfer and fits the whole chain, object, and dates; a skipped link jumps over a required owner or handoff, an ending names the object’s first known owner, and an undo returns the object to a prior owner or changes an earlier transfer.
sketches.move_shape: Name one next handoff: “Before Aunt Lina had it, the clock belonged to Cousin Mark, who traded it for a sandwich.”
sketches.first_card: A silver spoon at dinner has the family crest on it, though nobody agrees which family it belongs to.
